context_documents.title: One shared hand on a fixed inclined lift
context_documents.body:
# 2023-1746: One shared hand on a fixed inclined lift

Version: DCMP/Worlds rebuild as recalled by Jack Sarratt; exact installation dates unaudited

## Evidence premises

- **owner_firsthand_account**: Fixed approximately 30–45 degree four-stage elevator; shared cone/cube hand on a wrist; ground pickup and placement use that hand. Stage-count convention and angle reference remain unmeasured. Locator: Conversation supplied by Jack Sarratt, 2026-11-07
- **independent_source_partial_correspondence**: Later IRI interview describes a compact continuously rigged elevator and shared intake. It supports the family, not exact DCMP hardware identity. Locator: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PhlmMCOir8&t=98

## Piece flow

Owner-described direct path: ground piece → roller hand → retained in that hand while wrist and carriage move → scoring release. Zero intermediate handoff on this described main path. Roller rotation is still a powered function; eliminating a handoff does not eliminate acquisition control.

## Physical arrangement and swept space

An inclined mast occupies a fixed diagonal corridor above the chassis. The carriage carries the wrist and hand along that corridor. The wrist swings the mouth toward the floor and then to a travel or placing orientation. The hand, held piece and any protruding cone sweep beyond the carriage; their clearance must be checked at every lift position. Mast feet must react overturning loads into the chassis. Battery access, exact mounting coordinates and measured extension envelope are not established.

## Independent motions and powered functions

Conditional kinematic model: one coordinated lift coordinate plus wrist rotation; roller spin handles piece transport. Four stages are not automatically four independently controlled degrees of freedom. Count drive translation/yaw separately and do not infer motor count from stages. Coupling/rigging details of the recalled configuration are unknown.

## Burdens avoided

The shared hand avoids transferring possession between a dedicated ground collector and scoring device on this path. A fixed mast avoids a powered shoulder angle. Fewer pose combinations can reduce collision planning and calibration work.

## Burdens retained

The driver must place the shared mouth close enough to the piece. Carriage stroke couples vertical height and horizontal reach. Mast compliance, stage friction, roller contact, cone orientation, wrist holding torque, loaded CG and driver alignment remain real costs. Low independent motion count does not establish easy fabrication or a light complete robot.

## Engineering hypothesis

If the task poses lie near the fixed mast trajectory and wrist reach, the architecture can obtain needed capability with fewer independent coordinates. Keeping possession in one hand removes an interface where timing, compression and support must otherwise agree. This is a plausible engineering mechanism, not a measured explanation of the season result.

## Rival explanation

Driver practice, autonomous execution, matchups, alliance partners and service quality can explain high results without proving architectural superiority. A more articulated robot might recover from more pickup orientations or reach a scoring pose with less chassis repositioning.

## When the preference reverses

The advantage reverses if floor capture requires slow precise alignment, mast/chassis positioning costs more time than a reliable handoff, or reach/stow/charge-station envelopes force bad routes. A wider collector can be worthwhile if acquisition dominates complete cycles.

## Unknowns

Exact angle, stage nomenclature, stroke, mass distribution, cone pickup orientations, handoff alternatives, battery route and dated cubeapult installation. The owner vision counterfactual and top-15–25 ranking are opinions, not predicted outcomes.

## Proposed check; not performed

First overlay required pickup, transit and scoring poses on a side-view layout. Then compare the distribution of approach-to-secure times and complete-cycle times against a wide-collector alternative, including failed pickups. Do not build both full robots to answer a geometry question.

## Outcome evidence

No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.

## Sources

- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PhlmMCOir8

context_documents.title: A small extra mechanism with a specific autonomous job
context_documents.body:
# 2023-1746: A small extra mechanism with a specific autonomous job

Version: IRI interview published July 2023; not backdated to DCMP

## Evidence premises

- **team_interview_caption_paraphrase**: Team describes thinner 1-inch elevator tubing to reduce high-mounted weight, custom bearing blocks and a continuously rigged belt. Locator: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PhlmMCOir8&t=98
- **team_interview_caption_paraphrase**: Shared intake draws on 111, with a separately inspired wrist. Team discusses practice and wrist tuning. Locator: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PhlmMCOir8&t=209
- **team_interview_caption_paraphrase**: A servo-released over-center cube launcher avoids an initial autonomous turn; high/low targets depend on routine. Exact accuracy was not measured in this review. Locator: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PhlmMCOir8&t=506

## Piece flow

The normal shared-hand path remains separate from the launcher path. For the described autonomous feature a human preloads a cube on the launcher; release sends it rearward, allowing the robot to continue its route. Do not draw an invented automatic handoff from the roller hand into the launcher.

## Physical arrangement and swept space

Reserve a rearward launch corridor, the cocked linkage envelope and safe preload access. This is a second scoring path occupying frame space even though it does not require another continuously positioned arm. Exact location, energy storage, latch loads and full return procedure are not reconstructed from captions.

## Independent motions and powered functions

Lift, wrist and rollers serve the main path; a servo triggers the auxiliary launcher. A binary release adds a control state and hardware even if it adds no continuously controlled positioning axis. Do not call the whole robot a two-motor mechanism.

## Burdens avoided

A dedicated preloaded release can avoid spending drivetrain time on a turn. It also avoids requiring the main hand to execute that first rearward scoring operation.

## Burdens retained

Preload orientation, latch repeatability, launch dispersion, game legality, reset effort and autonomous start alignment now matter. A short mechanism can create a large reliability cost if it needs delicate setup. Interview tuning/practice comments contradict any claim that simple hardware needs no integration work.

## Engineering hypothesis

The relevant question is marginal autonomous score per occupied space, setup time and failure exposure. A small additional mechanism can strengthen a simple architecture when it removes a specific route penalty and leaves the ordinary cycle path uncomplicated.

## Rival explanation

An improved start pose, different route or more accurate chassis control might recover the same time without the launcher. Interview success reports are not a comparison against those alternatives.

## When the preference reverses

Remove or redesign it if the autonomous gain disappears under legal starts, its preload disrupts setup, it blocks service, or miss cost outweighs the extra piece. Retain useful complexity when measured gain survives these conditions.

## Unknowns

Installation chronology, stored-energy details, exact repeatability and whether a three-piece routine was consistently achieved. Captions are automatic and can misrecognize names/numerals; no continuous video or CAD review is claimed.

## Proposed check; not performed

Compare legal autonomous route budgets with and without the initial turn using existing path/layout tools; only if this changes the choice, test a small launcher for dispersion and preload sensitivity.

## Outcome evidence

No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.

## Sources

- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PhlmMCOir8

source_reviews.title: OTTO at IRI
source_reviews.locator: 1:08–1:37 drive; 1:39–3:12 elevator; 3:15–5:24 intake and wrist; 5:27–8:20 controls; 8:26–10:00 autonomous preload
source_reviews.review_basis: Read available English captions of the team interview. Times refer to the source video.
facts: Team describes mostly stock Mk4i L1 swerve, a continuously rigged compact elevator and one cone/cube tool.
The later IRI elevator used one-inch tubing and custom guides after the team found its earlier structure carried too much mass high.
The team demonstrated cone and cube acquisition at the single substation and described a servo-triggered cube launcher for autonomous.
source_reviews.limitations: IRI is a later snapshot. The field record and interview do not establish every DCMP/Worlds component or the exact earlier mast angle.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: The core OTTO design uses the same roller hand to acquire and place either game piece. In the owner’s account of the DCMP/Worlds rebuild, the hand rides a four-stage fixed inclined elevator and rotates on a wrist. The mast supplies height and reach together, while the wrist changes tool orientation. The later IRI interview confirms the compact continuously rigged lift and shared hand in that later configuration. It also describes the earlier, taller machine and the changes made to take weight out of the top. The separate autonomous cube launcher serves one preload task. The normal piece cycle can still stay in one hand.
piece_flow: The driver aligns the mouth to the piece. The owner describes floor pickup with the wrist lowered. The IRI interview shows the single-substation method where the driver brings the robot flush to the wall and a human player supplies the piece.
The rollers pull the piece into the hand and retain it while the lift and wrist move toward the scoring pose. The hand releases the cone or cube at the target.
The lift and wrist return toward the acquisition pose. The autonomous preload launcher follows a separate path and avoids an initial chassis turn in some routines.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: On a fixed inclined mast, every increment of travel changes both the tool’s height and its horizontal position. Layout begins with floor, loading, transit and scoring poses with the actual piece installed. Place the mast and wrist pivots so the chassis can reach all essential poses without using extra reverse or steering moves. The early high-mass design is a useful reminder that a mechanically simple architecture still requires a loaded stability check.

subsystems.name: Chassis and approach
subsystems.construction: The interview describes Mk4i L1 modules with minimal modification.
subsystems.operation: Drive the single tool to the floor, station or scoring approach that its workspace can reach.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team preferred available drive torque for its reported robot weight and defense.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Direct acquisition shifts some workload from mechanism alignment to driver positioning. Evaluate time from first sight of the piece to confirmed capture, including failed approaches.
subsystems.interfaces: The mast line and bumper face constrain how close the rollers can reach the wall and floor.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: A bumper offset, arm zero change or poor alignment can show up as an acquisition problem even when roller speed is unchanged.
subsystems.unknowns: No measured turning, loaded acceleration or capture tolerance comparison.

subsystems.name: Continuously rigged elevator
subsystems.construction: The IRI team describes one-inch thin-wall tubing, custom Thrifty-inspired bearing blocks and a continuous belt.
subsystems.operation: Move the roller hand along the mast and hold each scoring height with closed-loop control.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team reduced high weight after its first version was too tall and heavy.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A fixed mast removes a shoulder axis and makes packaging easier to reason about. It couples horizontal and vertical motion, so practical reach depends on the chassis pose.
subsystems.interfaces: Guide and belt loads change with tool extension. Belt tension, carriage yaw and wrist cable clearance matter through the entire stroke.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check binding and belt tracking with an off-center cone and inspect where the mast lands under bump contact.
subsystems.unknowns: The earlier rebuild angle and stage terminology come from owner recollection. The later interview supplies different evidence.

subsystems.name: Shared wrist and roller hand
subsystems.construction: The team credits 111 for the roller intake inspiration and 1339 for the wrist approach. A Falcon drives through gearing and chain. The tool uses machined polycarbonate and printed parts.
subsystems.operation: Rotate to the pickup pose, draw a cone or cube into the tool, hold possession through the lift movement and release at the node.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team selected the intake after seeing reliable use elsewhere. The wrist reduction gives useful holding torque.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: One possession path removes the timing and alignment demands of an intake-to-gripper handoff. It still needs a workable grip on both pieces and a wrist that holds position at load without excess current.
subsystems.interfaces: Tool width and cone orientation determine the practical floor and pole approach. The wrist and carriage must support the heaviest useful extension.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Inspect wear at the roller surface, chain tension and flex in the tool plates. Compare acquisition at multiple piece orientations.
subsystems.unknowns: The full wrist reduction and field capture envelope remain unresolved.

subsystems.name: Autonomous preload and controls
subsystems.construction: Servo releases an over-center preload launcher. The lift and wrist hold targets with closed-loop control.
subsystems.operation: The launcher scores a staged cube rearward in the chosen autonomous routine, then normal acquisition uses the shared hand.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team described saving time otherwise lost to turning.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A narrow autonomous exception can earn its complexity when it bypasses a repeatable dead movement. Count reset time, preload reliability and changes to the starting pose.
subsystems.interfaces: The preload launcher must coexist with the lift and remain clear of the normal cycle. The wrist’s higher torque and gravity load change tuning demands.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Test scoring from modest pose error and confirm a failed preload leaves the rest of the autonomous routine useful.
subsystems.unknowns: The interview reports success qualitatively. It gives no matched comparison of all autos or a measured vision upgrade effect.

revisions: Earlier tall structure gave way to the compact lift described at IRI.
The owner describes DCMP/Worlds fixed incline and shared hand. The IRI interview has its own configuration scope.
The autonomous preload path was added to eliminate a turn in selected starts.
transferable_principles: Plot the required possession poses against one constrained lift path before adding an arm axis.
Compare actual failed pickups and approach correction time before deciding whether a separate collector earns a handoff.
Validate low mass and simple load paths with the piece installed at the worst pose.
disconfirming_conditions: Add a separate collector when its increase in capture envelope repays the time and failure risk of the handoff.
An articulated arm can earn extra motion when the robot must reach from several chassis approaches or over large obstacles.
remaining_gaps: Exact 2023 DCMP and Worlds geometry and revision dates, complete field acquisition statistics, independently measured performance differences.
